label: cor:common-divisor
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor:common-divisor}
Over every characteristic zero field, $D$ divides every solution of
\eqref{eq:intro-cyclic}--\eqref{eq:intro-norm}. Up to a nonzero scalar,
it is the greatest common divisor of all nonzero solutions.
head: environment

title: Example
body_md:
The first nonzero solutions occur in degree ten. The two binary
polynomials in the original problem \cite[p.~481]{ABBI26} can be
written as
\begin{align*}
  q_{\mathrm s}(X,Y)
    &=XY(X^2-Y^2)^2(X^2-4Y^2)(4X^2-Y^2),\\
  q_{\mathrm a}(X,Y)
    &=X^2Y^2(X^2-Y^2)^3.
\end{align*}
Both satisfy \eqref{eq:normalized-period-space}.
The first is symmetric and odd in each variable, and the second is
alternating and even in each variable. Their cyclic sums
$f_{\mathrm s}=\Phi(q_{\mathrm s})$ and
$f_{\mathrm a}=\Phi(q_{\mathrm a})$ form a basis of $W_{10}(F)$.
Over $\mathbb C$, the binary polynomials $q_{\mathrm s}$ and
$q_{\mathrm a}$ are nonzero scalar multiples of the odd and
normalized even period polynomials, respectively, of Ramanujan's
weight twelve discriminant cusp form $\Delta(\tau)$.
head: environment

label: lem:sector-decomp
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:sector-decomp}
Homogeneous components of a solution are solutions. Its symmetric and
alternating parts $(f+Sf)/2$ and $(f-Sf)/2$ are also solutions. There are no
nonzero solutions of degree at most three.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Each operator in \eqref{eq:polynomial-operators} preserves degree. Direct
substitution gives $SAS=A^2$ and $SCS=C^{-1}$. Hence $S$ preserves both
conditions $Nf=0$ and $Cf=f$. A three-cycle and a transposition generate the
full permutation group, which proves the two symmetry assertions. In degrees zero and one, the cyclic spaces are spanned by $1$ and
$x+y+z$. Their norms are $3$ and $3z$, respectively. In degree two, the
basis $x^2+y^2+z^2,xy+yz+zx$ has norms
$4(x^2-xy+y^2)+3z^2,\quad x^2-xy+y^2$.
These are linearly independent. The kernels in degrees zero, one, and two are therefore zero.

In degree three, the symmetric basis
$p_3=x^3+y^3+z^3$, $m_{21}=x^2y+x^2z+xy^2+xz^2+y^2z+yz^2$, and $xyz$ has norms
\[
 3z^3,\qquad -(x+y)(2x-y)(x-2y)+4z(x^2-xy+y^2),
 \qquad z(x^2-xy+y^2),
\]
which are linearly independent. The alternating basis
$\Delta=(x-y)(x-z)(y-z)$ has norm $3xy(x-y)\ne0$.

label: lem:sym-boundary-factors
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Write $f\in V_n$, put $\nu=(-1)^n$, and let $g(s,t)=f(s,-s,t)$.
Expansion and symmetry give
\begin{align*}
 &(N_{23}f)(-s,-t,s)-\nu(N_{23}f)(-s-t,-t,s)\\
 &\quad \quad -(N_{23}f)(-s-t,-s,-s)+(N_{12}f)(-s-t,0,s)
   =\nu\{g(s,t)-g(s+t,t)\}.
\end{align*}
Therefore, $g$ is translation-invariant in $s$ over $\mathbb Q(t)$, hence constant in $s$.
The norm at $(0,0,t)$ makes it zero. Symmetry gives the three factors of $c_+$.
For even degree, put $h(s,t)=f(s,t,-s-t)$. The identity
\[
 (N_{12}f)(-s-t,t,s)-(N_{23}f)(-s-2t,-t,s)
     =h(s,t)-h(s+t,t)
\]
makes $h$ independent of $s$. Since $h(s,t)=h(t,s)$, it is constant.
Positive homogeneity gives $h=0$. The distinct linear factors are
relatively prime, which proves the product divisibility.

label: lem:period-extraction
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
We first read the first order data on $w=0$, then reconstruct a binary
period, and finally divide the remainder by $w^2$.

\smallskip\noindent\emph{The first order data.}
First, direct substitution gives $J_v(X,0,Z)=Z v(Z,-X,X)$. Thus $J_v=0$ implies vanishing
on each opposite pair plane, and hence $c_+\mid v$.
Write $\partial_i$ for differentiation in the $i$th argument of $v$, and put
\[
 h(X,Y)=v(-Y,X,Y-X),\quad
 H(X,Y)=(\partial_1+\partial_2)v(-Y,X,Y-X),\quad
 p(X,Y)=-\int_0^X H(s,Y)\,ds.
\]
Define
\[
 C_v(X,Y)=p(X-Y,Y)-p(X,Y)-h(X,Y),\qquad
 \mathcal D=-Y\partial_X,\qquad \tau=e^{\mathcal D}.
\]
The operator $\tau$ translates $X$ to $X-Y$. We claim that
\begin{equation}\label{eq:normal-jet}
 J_v(X,Y,3Y)=0,\qquad
 \left.\partial_ZJ_v\right|_{Z=3Y}
     =\tau^2 B(3\mathcal D)B(\mathcal D)C_v.
\end{equation}
Here all power series are finite operators on the fixed polynomial degree.
To verify the claim, let $v_i=(\partial_i v)(-Y,X,Y-X)$ and set
$\psi_i^0=\psi_i|_{Z=3Y}$,
$\psi_i^1=(\partial_Z\psi_i)|_{Z=3Y}$. Odd homogeneity and symmetry give
\[
 \psi_1^0=-h,\quad \psi_2^0=-(1+\tau+\tau^2)h,\qquad
 \psi_1^1=v_1,\quad \psi_2^1=(1+\tau)v_1-\tau^2v_3.
\]
The chain rule also gives $h_X=v_2-v_3$, $h_Y=-v_1+v_3$, and $p_X=-(v_1+v_2)$.
Differentiate the defining expression for $J_v$, including its Bernoulli
operator. The required cancellations are exactly
\begin{align*}
 B(3t)(1+e^t+e^{2t})&=3B(t),\\
 -B(t)+tB'(3t)(1+e^t+e^{2t})+te^{2t}B(3t)
     &=-e^{2t}B(3t)B(t),\\
 B(\mathcal D)(\tau-1)&=\mathcal D.
\end{align*}
The first two identities follow by substituting $B(t)=t/(e^t-1)$ and
clearing denominators. The third is its defining finite-difference identity.
This proves \eqref{eq:normal-jet}. The operator on its right is invertible,
since each factor has constant term one. Consequently $J_v=0$ gives $C_v=0$.

\smallskip\noindent\emph{Reconstruction of the binary period.}
Symmetry and homogeneity give
\begin{equation}\label{eq:H-symmetry}
 h_X=H(X,Y)-H(Y-X,Y),\qquad H(-Y,-X)=H(X,Y).
\end{equation}
Differentiate $C_v=0$ in $X$ and use the first identity to obtain
$H(-X,Y)=H(X,Y)$. Since $H$ has even total degree, it is separately even
and symmetric. Thus $p$ is odd in $X$ and even in $Y$, and
$p_X(X,Y)=p_X(Y,-X)$. Define
\begin{equation}\label{eq:q-extract}
 q(X,Y)=-\frac{Xp(Y,-X)+Yp(X,Y)}{m+1}.
\end{equation}
Euler's identity for the degree $m$ polynomial $p$ gives $q_Y=-p$.
The displayed formula and the parities of $p$ show that $q$ is symmetric,
odd in each variable, and zero on both axes. Since $c_+\mid v$, we have
$h(0,Y)=0$. Evaluating $C_v=0$ at $X=0$ therefore gives $p(Y,Y)=0$,
and hence $q(Y,Y)=0$.

Set
\[
 D_q=q(X,Y)-q(X-Y,Y)+q(X,X-Y).
\]
Using $q_Y=-p$, symmetry of $q$, and oddness of $p$ in its first
variable, we obtain
\[
 (\partial_X+\partial_Y)D_q
 =-p(Y,X)-p(X,Y)+p(X-Y,Y)-p(X-Y,X)
 =h(X,Y)+h(Y,X)=0.
\]
Here $C_v=0$ gives the second equality. A homogeneous polynomial of degree $m+1$
annihilated by this derivative is a multiple of $(X-Y)^{m+1}$.
At $Y=0$ it equals $q(X,X)=0$. Thus $D_q$ vanishes, which proves
$q\in\mathcal B_{m+1}$.

\smallskip\noindent\emph{The lift and descent in degree.}
We check directly that every lift has zero obstruction. For
$q\in\mathcal B_d$, put $t=Z-2Y$ and
$r(X,Y,Z)=q(X,Y)-q(X,t)$. If $\tau_u$ translates $X$ to $X-u$, the two
frame polynomials of $\Phi(q)$ are
\[
 ((1-\tau_Y)r,\ (1-\tau_Z)r).
\]
This follows by expanding the three cyclic sums and using
\eqref{eq:binary-addition}. Since
$B(-u\partial_X)(1-\tau_u)=u\partial_X$, the two terms of
$J_{\Phi(q)}$ cancel. The identity $\Phi(q)=wL(q)$ and
\eqref{eq:J-w-mult} then give $J_{L(q)}=0$.
Cancellation on each opposite pair plane also gives $c_+\mid L(q)$.

The polynomial extracted from $L(q)$ is the original $q$. Indeed,
differentiate $\Phi(q)=wL(q)$ once in each of the first two variables
and restrict to $w=0$. The resulting first-plane data give
$p_{L(q)}=-q_Y$, which recovers \eqref{eq:q-extract}.
For a symmetric positive degree homogeneous polynomial, $p_v=0$ is
equivalent to $w^2\mid v$: its three pair sums of first derivatives
then vanish on $w=0$, so twice each individual derivative vanishes there.
Euler's identity gives $w\mid v$, and differentiation gives a second
factor of $w$. The converse is immediate.
It follows that $v-L(q)=w^2u$. The quotient $u$ is symmetric and satisfies
$J_u=0$ by \eqref{eq:J-w-mult}. Repeat in degree $m-2$. The final remainder
has degree below three and is divisible by $c_+$, so it is zero.
The extracted first-plane data at each step also prove uniqueness.

title: Corollary

title: Proof
body_md:
For $n=0$, the assertion follows from Lemma~\ref{lem:sector-decomp}.
Assume $n>0$. In even degree, Lemma~\ref{lem:sym-boundary-factors} gives $f=wv$ with
$v$ symmetric of odd degree. Equation~\eqref{eq:J-w-mult} gives $J_v=0$.
Apply Lemma~\ref{lem:period-extraction} and multiply its expansion by $w$.
In odd degree apply that lemma directly to $f$.

label: lem:outer-values
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:outer-values}
If $h$ is a normalized level one cusp eigenform of weight $k>6$, then
$L(h,k-2)$ and $L(h,k-1)$ are nonzero. The same holds after omitting any
finite set of Euler factors.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The Fourier coefficient integral at height $y=1/m$ and the bound
$y^{k/2}|h(\tau)|\ll1$ give $a_h(m)=O(m^{k/2})$.
Thus the Dirichlet series converges absolutely for $\Re s>k/2+1$.
To check each local denominator as well, the Hecke recurrence gives
\[
 \sum_{r\ge0}a_h(p^r)t^r=(1-a_h(p)t+p^{k-1}t^2)^{-1}.
\]
The coefficient bound makes this holomorphic for $|t|<p^{-k/2}$.
Consequently, if the denominator is $(1-\alpha_pt)(1-\beta_pt)$, then
$|\alpha_p|,|\beta_p|\le p^{k/2}$. Each local factor is therefore finite
and nonzero for $\Re s>k/2$. In the smaller half-plane
$\Re s>k/2+1$, the sum over primes of the absolute deviations of the
local denominators from one converges. Their product is nonzero there.
Since $k-2>k/2+1$ when $k>6$, both asserted values lie in that half-plane.
Removing finitely many nonzero factors preserves nonvanishing.

label: thm:good-apartment
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{thm:good-apartment}
The graph $\mathcal T^\uparrow$ is connected, and we have
\begin{equation}\label{eq:good-apartment-presentation}
 \operatorname{St}^\uparrow\cong
 \frac{\mathbb Q K}{\mathbb Q K(1+A+A^2)+\mathbb Q K(C-1)+\mathbb Q K(S_0+1)}.
\end{equation}
Evaluation on the identity apartment gives isomorphisms
\[
 \operatorname{Hom}_K(\operatorname{St}^\uparrow,E_{n,0})\cong W_n^{\mathrm{alt}}(\mathbb Q),
 \qquad
 \operatorname{Hom}_K(\operatorname{St}^\uparrow,E_{n,1})\cong W_n^{\mathrm{sym}}(\mathbb Q).
\]
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
A partial augmented frame is a subset of an integral basis, possibly
together with one additional primitive line represented by a signed sum of
two basis vectors. Let $Y$ be the full good subcomplex of the complex of
partial augmented frames of Church--Putman
\cite[Theorem C]{ChurchPutman}. It is connected
and has $H_1(Y;\mathbb Q)=H_2(Y;\mathbb Q)=0$. Appendix~\ref{app:topology}
proves the required restriction argument. If $Y^0$ consists of simplices spanning
proper subspaces, pass to the poset of its nonempty simplices, ordered
by inclusion. The span map takes this poset to the poset of good proper
rational subspaces. The inverse image of the lower interval at a line is
a point. At a plane it is the face poset of its good filled Farey complex.
These spaces are contractible by Appendix~\ref{app:topology}. Quillen's
Theorem A~\cite{Quillen}, applied to these posets, gives a homotopy equivalence
of their order complexes and hence a
$K$-equivariant homology identification $H_1(Y^0;\mathbb Q)=\operatorname{St}^\uparrow$.
The relative complex of $(Y,Y^0)$ starts in degree two. Its generators are
good unimodular frames, and its relations are good augmented frames.

Every good primitive line has a unique primitive integral representative of $\ell$-value $1$
modulo three. Normalized good bases are therefore a single $K$-orbit.
In a good augmented core, reduction modulo three forces all signs in its
three-vector relation to agree. The normalized vectors sum to zero.
For $r=-e_1-e_2$, its boundary, modulo proper-span faces, is
$\partial[r,e_1,e_2,e_3]=[I]+[A]+[A^2]$.
Column permutations give $C-1$ and $S_0+1$. The relative homology sequence
now gives \eqref{eq:good-apartment-presentation}, and also connectedness
of $Y^0$. The determinant twist reverses the transposition condition on
the polynomial. Finally $A^{-1}=A^2$, so the left-action norm is the same
polynomial norm.

label: prop:26-model
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $E=E_{n,t}$. Rational Borel--Serre duality gives
\[
 H^3(K,E^*)\cong(\operatorname{St}\otimes E^*)_K,
 \qquad H_3(K,E)\cong\operatorname{Hom}_K(\operatorname{St},E),
\]
where the second isomorphism is obtained by dualizing the first,
with the coefficient conventions fixed above. The virtual cohomological
dimension is three, and the orientation character is trivial
\cite{BorelSerre}. Induction over the finite coset space
$K\backslash G$ identifies the latter space with $G$-equivariant
maps from $\operatorname{St}$ to the induced coefficient module
\cite[Chapter~III, Section~5]{Brown}.

The full apartment presentation \cite[Theorem~B]{ChurchPutman}
has signed-permutation relations and the relation $1+A+A^2$.
The first says that $F\mid_t h=\operatorname{sgn}(\pi)F$, which is
\eqref{eq:fiber-signed}. The second says that
$F+F\mid_t A+F\mid_t A^2=0$, which is \eqref{eq:fiber-norm}
after evaluating at $r$. These relations are sufficient by the
presentation theorem. Under induction, the identity coset is indexed
by $\ell$, so evaluation there recovers the original apartment value.
Lemma~\ref{lem:apartment-boundary-pairing} fixes the geometric
normalization of this evaluation.

label: lem:apartment-boundary-pairing
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Intersection with the flat reads the top-cell coefficient. Moving the
intersection into a boundary collar gives the bottom arrow.

For the first, normalize a form in the standard open top cell by requiring
that $e_1,e_2,e_3$ have length one. Near the identity matrix its Gram matrix
is
\[
 \begin{pmatrix}1&r_{12}&r_{13}\\r_{12}&1&r_{23}\\r_{13}&r_{23}&1\end{pmatrix}.
\]
The diagonal flat meets this cell at the identity, transversely. It meets no
other open top cell: a diagonal form is well rounded only when all three
diagonal entries agree, and at that form the shortest primitive vectors
are precisely $\pm e_i$. The off-diagonal coordinates orient the cell,
and the two diagonal ratios orient the flat. A permutation has its permutation
sign on the cell, while a coordinate sign change has sign $+1$, exactly as
in the top-cell model. The local intersection therefore evaluates the
coefficient by $\varphi$.

Translate this calculation by an integral basis matrix. The cellular
orientation and the dual coefficient transport are respectively the signed
permutation character and $\varphi\cdot g$. Thus the local intersections
assemble with the same relations as the modular symbol pairing
\cite[Section 3, (3--1)]{AllisonAshConrad}. With induced coefficients,
unfolding a chain over $K\backslash G$ labels the translated basis by its
covector $\ell g$. The functional $\varphi_\lambda$ selects the identity
coset, not the sum of all covectors. Hence the intersection of $z$ with
$a_\varphi$ is $\varphi(F_z)$.

For the second comparison, smooth the neat cover's corners and move $c$
slightly inward along a collar, transverse to the relative flat.
The intersections are those of $c$ with the flat's boundary. With the
boundary orientation induced by this collar, the cap-product definition
gives $\langle\operatorname{PD}_{\partial}c,\partial a_\varphi\rangle$.
The identity holds on chains modulo boundaries by naturality of
Poincar\'e--Lefschetz duality \cite{BorelSerre}.

Both constructions commute with coefficient transport and subdivision.
Coset unfolding is the cellular Shapiro map, proving compatibility with
induction. Taking finite group coinvariants in homology and invariants
in cohomology is exact and preserves the pairing, giving descent to the
stated level.
head: environment

label: thm:boundary-evaluation
title: Proposition
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
\smallskip\noindent\emph{Passage to the boundary.}
Choose a neat normal subgroup $\Gamma'\subset K\cap\operatorname{SL}_3(\mathbb Z)$ and put
$X_{\Gamma'}=\Gamma'\backslash\mathscr X$.
Proposition~\ref{ar:prop:coercivity}, proved in
Appendix~\ref{app:arithmetic-direct}, gives
\[
 H_c^2(X_{\Gamma'},E_{n,t}\otimes\mathbb C)
       \longrightarrow H^2(X_{\Gamma'},E_{n,t}\otimes\mathbb C)
       \quad\text{equal to zero}.
\]
Extension to $\mathbb C$ is faithful, so the rational map is zero as well.

The five-dimensional symmetric space has trivial orientation character:
on symmetric matrices $Q\mapsto g^{\mathsf t}Qg$ has determinant
$(\det g)^4>0$, and quotienting by positive scaling removes an oriented
radial direction. Poincar\'e--Lefschetz duality identifies the
absolute-to-relative map in degree three homology with the zero map
above. Hence boundary homology surjects onto ordinary top homology.
Put $\Delta=K/\Gamma'$. 
Rational Hochschild--Serre and averaging give
\[
 H_3(K,E_{n,t})\cong H_3(\Gamma',E_{n,t})_{\Delta}.
\]
The same finite-cover descent applies to boundary homology and commutes with
its map to ordinary homology, so exact averaging preserves the
surjection at level $K$. It remains to evaluate an arbitrary boundary
class.

\smallskip\noindent\emph{Face cocycles and radical invariance.}
For evaluation, use $M=\operatorname{Ind}_K^G E_{n,t}$ and
$\partial=\partial\overline{\mathscr X}_G$ as in
Lemma~\ref{lem:apartment-boundary-pairing}. Shapiro's finite covector factor
retains every level three cusp. The two maximal parabolic types for $G$
are represented by the upper integral parabolics $P$ and $Q$ of block types
$(2,1)$ and $(1,2)$, with intersection the Borel group $B_0$.

Take collar neighborhoods of the two unions of closed maximal faces on
the neat cover. Their intersections are Borel strata, with no triple
intersection because a flag has only a line and a plane. Induction and
Shapiro give the Mayer--Vietoris sequence
\begin{equation}\label{eq:MV-boundary}
  H^0(P,M)\oplus H^0(Q,M)\to H^0(B_0,M)\to H^1(\partial,M)
  \to H^1(P,M)\oplus H^1(Q,M)\to H^1(B_0,M).
\end{equation}
To keep the corner signs explicit, use the mapping cone
\[
\begin{gathered}
 \mathcal C^r=C^r(P,M)\oplus C^r(Q,M)\oplus C^{r-1}(B_0,M),\\
 d(a,b,c)=(da,db,\operatorname{Res} a-\operatorname{Res} b-dc).
\end{gathered}
\]
The dual chain differential is
$\partial(x,y,z)=(\partial x+i_Pz,\partial y-i_Qz,-\partial z)$, where $i_P,i_Q$ are the two inclusions. The evaluation pairing is the sum
of the three component pairings. These differentials are adjoint. In
particular a degree-one cocycle is $(A_P,A_Q,u)$ with
$du=\operatorname{Res} A_P-\operatorname{Res} A_Q$.
For $R=P$ or $Q$, let $N_R\cong\mathbb Z^2$ be its unipotent radical and
$L_R$ its Levi quotient. The
five-term sequence shows
\begin{equation}\label{eq:inflated}
 H^1(R,M)=H^1(L_R,M^{N_R}).
\end{equation}
This means that face cocycles may be chosen to factor through the Levi,
with values fixed by the radical. We verify the necessary vanishing.
Decompose the covectors into $N_R$-orbits and apply Shapiro to their
stabilizer lattices. Their unipotent coefficient systems satisfy the
nilmanifold comparison \cite[Theorem~1.1]{Kasuya}. Lie and group cohomology
therefore agree, naturally for the Levi action, as explained in
Appendix~\ref{ar:sec:constantterms}. We may compute after complexification,
which detects the required rational vanishing.

We now compute the Lie cohomology explicitly. For the root operators $z\partial_x,z\partial_y$, the cocycle equation
for a pair $(a,b)$ is $a_y=b_x$. Such a pair is the gradient of a homogeneous
potential of degree $n+1$. Exact pairs are the gradients of potentials
divisible by $z$, so the quotient is the binary symmetric power of degree
$n+1$. For $x\partial_z,y\partial_z$, subtract an exact pair to remove
its common $z$-dependent part. The remaining binary pairs are taken modulo
$(xg,yg)$, and $(a,b)\mapsto xb-ya$ identifies that quotient with binary
forms of degree $n+1$. These descriptions cover the standard and dual
coefficient conventions.

It remains to take Levi invariants. In either case $H^1(N_R,E_{n,t})$ restricts to $\operatorname{Sym}^{n+1}(\mathbb Q^2)$ or its dual on the
derived subgroup $\mathrm{SL}_2$ of the Levi. The corresponding
level three subgroup fixes every covector. Its two opposite root
unipotents have no common invariant in this positive binary degree.
Consequently $H^1(N_R,M)^{L_R}$ vanishes, which proves \eqref{eq:inflated}.

If $v\in M^{N_R}$, the lattice fixing $\ell$ contains $3N_R$ and is
Zariski dense in the algebraic radical. Therefore $v(\ell)$ is invariant
under its root derivatives and belongs to $U_n$. The same conclusion holds
for invariants of the common root subgroup of two adjacent maximal radicals.

\smallskip\noindent\emph{Evaluation on the coordinate apartment.}
Let $c$ be a boundary top class and $z_c=F_{j_*c}$ its induced top-cell
coefficient. Let $U_n^\perp=\{\lambda\in V_n^*: \lambda|_{U_n}=0\}$.
To prove $z_c(\ell)\in U_n$, take $\lambda\in U_n^\perp$ and
put $\Phi_\lambda(v)=\lambda(v(\ell))$.
Lemma~\ref{lem:apartment-boundary-pairing} gives
\[
 \lambda(z_c(\ell))=\langle\omega,\partial a_{\Phi_\lambda}\rangle,
 \qquad \omega=\operatorname{PD}_{\partial}c\in H^1(\partial,M).
\]
The boundary apartment has successive vertices
$L_1,\ P_{12},\ L_2,\ P_{23},\ L_3,\ P_{31},\ L_1$,
where $L_i=\mathbb Q e_i$ and $P_{ij}=\mathbb Q e_i+\mathbb Q e_j$.
We evaluate its face and corner terms in the mapping-cone convention above.

By \eqref{eq:inflated}, a mapping-cone representative of $\omega$ is
$(A_P,A_Q,u)$, where the face cocycles are inflated and
$du=\operatorname{Res} A_P-\operatorname{Res} A_Q$. Here are the coefficient transports on the six
edges. For an ordered permutation $\sigma$, let $g_\sigma e_i=e_{\sigma(i)}$.
Starting from the flag $L_1\subset P_{12}$, the permutations are
\[
 (1,2,3),\quad(2,1,3),\quad(2,3,1),\quad
 (3,2,1),\quad(3,1,2),\quad(1,3,2),
\]
with incidence signs $+,-,+,-,+,-$, respectively. The transported dual
coefficient is $\Phi_\lambda\cdot g_\sigma$. The left action inside this
formula includes the determinant twist. The listed signs are the separate
cellular orientation signs. Every $g_\sigma$ fixes $\ell$ and preserves
$U_n$. Each transported coefficient therefore annihilates the appropriate
radical invariant space, and all face pairings are zero. Further transport
within a maximal parabolic preserves that space.

For a corner, the common root group is a translate of
$N_0=\{I+aE_{13}:a\in\mathbb Z\}$. Its coefficient functional annihilates
$M^{N_0}$, and finite-dimensional duality gives
$(M^{N_0})^\perp =\operatorname{span}\{\Psi\cdot n-\Psi:n\in N_0,\ \Psi\in M^*\}$.
Thus the corner zero-chain can be written
$r=\sum_i(\Psi_i\cdot n_i-\Psi_i)$, with $n_i\in N_0$. In the right-module
bar complex, $\partial(\Psi[n])=\Psi\cdot n-\Psi$, so
$s=\sum_i\Psi_i[n_i]$ has $\partial s=r$. Both face cocycles are inflated
from their Levis and vanish on this common radical. Adjointness gives
\[
 \langle u,r\rangle
 =\sum_i\Psi_i(n_i\cdot u-u)
 =\langle du,s\rangle
 =\langle\operatorname{Res} A_P-\operatorname{Res} A_Q,s\rangle=0.
\]
Hence, the corner pairing vanishes by the coboundary equation for $u$
(no invariance of $u$ is required).
We obtain $\lambda(z_c(\ell))=0$ for every annihilator $\lambda$, so
$z_c(\ell)\in U_n$. Lemma~\ref{prop:26-model} completes the proof.

label: lem:bad-line-coordinate
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:bad-line-coordinate}
The restriction of $a_F$ to the bad-line stabilizer has only the mixed
Hochschild--Serre component. This component is cuspidal on the binary Levi.
If it is zero, then $J_f=0$ as a polynomial. In the coordinate
\eqref{eq:radical-coordinate}, its cocycle is the negative of the one
whose specified order three generator has value $J_f$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
\smallskip\noindent\emph{The radical coordinate.}
Choose the base vertex $v=G_0$ and the path $s:G_0\to\mathbb Q e_3\to H_0$, where
$G_0=\langle e_1,e_3\rangle$ and $H_0=\langle e_2,e_3\rangle$.
The bad-line Levi fixes $H_0$ and its radical $U$ fixes $G_0$.
For Levi elements $l$, use $\tau(l)=s-ls$ and $\tau(ul)=u\tau(l)$.
In particular $\tau(u)$ is zero. A binary Levi matrix $l$ acts on the last two
coordinates through $\operatorname{diag}(1,l)$. Put
\[
 A_0=\begin{pmatrix}1&-1\\3&-2\end{pmatrix},\quad
 B_0=\begin{pmatrix}-1&0\\-3&1\end{pmatrix},\quad
 R_0=\begin{pmatrix}-1&0\\0&1\end{pmatrix}.
\]
When acting on $\mathbb Q^3$, these binary matrices are embedded as
$\operatorname{diag}(1,g)$ in the bad-line Levi. Both $B_0,R_0$ fix $s$. The radical cocycle
$\phi_l(u)=F((u-1)\tau(l))$ therefore has zero values for these two Levi
elements. We make the path cancellation explicit. Put
\[
 a=e_3,\quad b=(1,1,2),\quad c=(0,1,2),\quad
 d=(1,0,1),\quad e=(2,1,2),\quad G'=\langle e_1,c\rangle.
\]
Vectors denote their rational lines. Since $A_0e_3=-c$
and $A_0H_0=H_0$, the path $\tau(A_0)=s-A_0s$ is
\[
 G_0\longrightarrow a\longrightarrow H_0\longrightarrow c
 \longrightarrow G'.
\]
For independent vectors $v,w$, write
$\mathfrak e(v,w)=[\mathbb Q v,\langle v,w\rangle]+[\langle v,w\rangle,\mathbb Q w]$.
The apartment convention is
$\mathcal A(v,w,t)=\mathfrak e(v,w)+\mathfrak e(w,t)+\mathfrak e(t,v)$.
Cancelling repeated edges in the two translated paths gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
 (U_{12}-1)\tau(A_0)&=\mathfrak e(a,b)+\mathfrak e(b,c)+\mathfrak e(c,a),\\
 (U_{13}-1)\tau(A_0)&=\mathfrak e(a,d)+\mathfrak e(d,e)
                  +\mathfrak e(e,c)+\mathfrak e(c,a).
\end{aligned}
\]
The lines $b,c,e$ lie in one plane, so
$\mathfrak e(e,b)+\mathfrak e(b,c)=\mathfrak e(e,c)$. Consequently the two translated paths reduce to apartments:
\begin{align*}
 (U_{12}-1)\tau(A_0)&=\mathcal A(e_3,(1,1,2),(0,1,2)),\\
 (U_{13}-1)\tau(A_0)&=\mathcal A(e_3,(1,1,2),(0,1,2))
 +\mathcal A(e_3,(1,0,1),(2,1,2))
       +\mathcal A(e_3,(2,1,2),(1,1,2)).
\end{align*}
The column-sign lists are $(1,-1,-1),(1,1,-1),(1,-1,-1)$.
By \eqref{eq:frame-evaluation}, the preceding apartment identities give
\[
 \phi_{A_0}(U_{12})=\psi_1,
 \qquad
 \phi_{A_0}(U_{13})=\psi_2,
\]
where $\psi_1,\psi_2$ are exactly the symmetric frame polynomials
in \eqref{eq:Jdef}. Applying the radical coordinate
\eqref{eq:radical-coordinate}, we obtain
\[
 \mathcal J(\phi_{A_0})
   =ZB(-Y\partial_X)\psi_1-YB(-Z\partial_X)\psi_2
   =J_f.
\]
Thus $J_f$ is the literal radical coordinate and is independent of $X$.
We write it as $J_f(Y,Z)$ for the rest of this proof.

The mixed bar edge of a two-cocycle is
$e(z)(l)(u)=z(l,l^{-1}ul)-z(u,l)$.
Our choices $\tau(u)=0$ and $\tau(ul)=u\tau(l)$ give
\[
\begin{aligned}
 z_F(l,l^{-1}ul)&=F(\tau(l)-u\tau(l))=-\phi_l(u) \qquad {\text {\rm and}}\qquad
 z_F(u,l)&=F(u\tau(l)-\tau(ul))=0.
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus the mixed edge is $-\phi_l(u)$ and $z_F|_{U\times U}=0$.
We retain this sign, though its reversal would not affect vanishing.
The Levi has rational cohomological dimension one, so no further
filtration term occurs in this kernel: the complete restriction lies in
$H^1(L,H^1(U,E_n))$.
Under $\operatorname{diag}(t,L)$ the coordinate
\eqref{eq:radical-coordinate} transforms by $J(v)\mapsto t^{-2}J(L^{-1}v)$.
Indeed inverse conjugation on the radical contributes $t^{-1}L$, the
coefficient action contributes $t^{-1}\det(L)^{-1}$, and the contraction
$(Z,-Y)$ contributes $\det L$. In particular the independent integral
line sign acts trivially.

\smallskip\noindent\emph{The binary quotient and its cusps.}

At each cusp we take translation coinvariants, then reflection invariants.

Write $C_m$ for the cyclic group of order $m$ and $\mathfrak S_3$ for
the permutation group on three letters. The remaining arithmetic group is
$\Gamma_2=\{g\in\mathrm{GL}_2(\mathbb Z):(0,1)g=(0,1)\pmod3\}$, and it has a presentation
\begin{equation}\label{eq:Gamma-presentation}
 \Gamma_2=\langle A_0,B_0\rangle*\langle R_0\rangle\cong\mathfrak S_3*C_2.
\end{equation}
To verify completeness, the determinant one subgroup maps injectively to
an index four subgroup of
$\mathrm{PSL}_2(\mathbb Z)=\operatorname{SL}_2(\mathbb Z)/\{\pm I_2\}\cong C_2*C_3$.
On its four cosets the two generators act with cycle types $(2,2)$ and
$(3,1)$. The Bass--Serre quotient has four edges and four vertices, one
$C_3$ vertex stabilizer, and all other stabilizers trivial. Schreier
reduction uses the standard matrices
$\mathsf S=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}0&-1\\1&0\end{smallmatrix}\right)$ and
$\mathsf T=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}1&1\\0&1\end{smallmatrix}\right)$.
The representatives $1,\mathsf S,\mathsf S\mathsf T,\mathsf S\mathsf T^2$ give
$\langle A_0,U_0\mid A_0^3=1\rangle$, where
$U_0=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}1&0\\3&1\end{smallmatrix}\right)$ and $A_0=U_0\mathsf T^{-1}$.
Matrix multiplication gives
$R_0U_0R_0=U_0^{-1}$ and
$R_0A_0R_0=U_0^{-1}A_0^{-1}U_0$.
Set $B_0=U_0R_0$ to obtain \eqref{eq:Gamma-presentation}, with no extra
mixed relation.

Transport to $(a,b)=(-Y,Z-2Y)$ and write
$\widehat J(a,b)=J_f(-a,b-2a)$. The actions become
$\mathcal A(a,b)=(-b,a-b)$, $\mathcal B(a,b)=(-a,b-a)$, and
$\mathcal R(a,b)=(-a,b-4a)$.
The positive cocycle $\mathcal J(\phi_l)$ has values $\widehat J,0,0$
on $A_0,B_0,R_0$. Their finite group relations give
$(1+\mathcal A+\mathcal A^2)\widehat J=0$ and
$\widehat J(a,b)=-\widehat J(b,a)$.
For $u=(2\widehat J+\mathcal A\widehat J)/3$, one has
$(1-\mathcal A)u=\widehat J$ and $\mathcal Bu=u$.
Thus in $V=\mathbb Q[a,b]_{n+1}$ the actual mixed class has quotient coordinate
\begin{equation}\label{eq:jF-quotient}
 j_F=-[u]\in V/(V^{\langle\mathcal A,\mathcal B\rangle}+V^{\mathcal R}).
\end{equation}
The minus sign comes from the mixed bar edge above.

Let $\Gamma_1(3)=\Gamma_2\cap\operatorname{SL}_2(\mathbb Z)$. A binary cusp is an orbit of
a rational line. There are exactly two cusp orbits, represented by the coordinate lines,
with widths one and three. Indeed a primitive column $(p,q)^t$ with
$3\mid q$ can be signed and completed to a matrix in $\Gamma_1(3)$ as its
first column. If $3\nmid q$, it can be so completed as its second column,
adjusting a Bezout complement by a multiple of that column.
These two cases are invariant and exhaustive.
Write $d=n+1$. At the lower cusp the translation is $Z\mapsto Z-3Y$,
whose degree $d$ coinvariant is the $Z^d$ coefficient. Its reflection fixes
that coefficient and reverses the translation, so its full cusp $H^1$
vanishes. At the upper cusp the translation is $Y\mapsto Y-Z$, with
coinvariant the $Y^d$ coefficient. The reflection acts on $H^1$ by
$(-1)^{d+1}$. Thus this restriction is automatically zero for even $d$.

For odd $d$, Lemma~\ref{lem:sym-boundary-factors} gives $w\mid f$.
All three frames have sum $Z-3Y$, so $J_f(Y,3Y)=0$, or
$\widehat J(a,-a)=0$. For the upper translation
$\mathcal A^2\mathcal B\mathcal R$, its cocycle value is
$\widehat J+\mathcal A\widehat J$. On $Z=0$, that is $b=2a$, the cocycle
relations give
$(\widehat J+\mathcal A\widehat J)(a,2a)=-\widehat J(a,-a)=0$.
Both cusp restrictions therefore vanish in every parity.

\smallskip\noindent\emph{Detection of the polynomial.}
Finally suppose $j_F=0$. Write the positive cocycle as $(1-l)m$.
Its zero values at $B_0,R_0$ make $m$ invariant under their product $U_0$,
hence $m=cY^d$. For odd $d$ the reflection makes $c=0$.
For even $d$, its $A_0$ value is
$J_f(Y,Z)=c(Y^d-(-2Y+Z)^d)$.
But $J_f(0,Z)=Zf(Z,-X,X)$ vanishes by the opposite pair vanishing.
Thus $c=0$ here as well. This proves the detection assertion.
head: environment

label: thm:J-vanishes
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{thm:J-vanishes}
Every symmetric homogeneous solution satisfies $J_f=0$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The degrees at most three are zero by Lemma~\ref{lem:sector-decomp}.
For $n\ge4$, let $a_F$ be the connecting class, and complexify its
coefficient system. Vanishing after complexification implies rational
vanishing. The class restricts to zero at every good vertex. Its bad-line
restriction is mixed and cuspidal by Lemma~\ref{lem:bad-line-coordinate}.
Its restriction at each flag is therefore zero: a flag contains either a
good line, where the whole restriction vanishes, or a bad line, where it
is a binary cusp restriction of that mixed class.

Let $P_0$ be the stabilizer of the bad plane $\langle e_1,e_2\rangle$ in
$K^\dagger$. Its radical is $N_P=\langle U_{13},U_{23}\rangle$, and its
Levi quotient is $L_P\cong\operatorname{GL}_2(\mathbb Z)$. The same gradient calculation used
in the support proof gives
\[
 H^1(N_P,E_n)=\det^{-1}\operatorname{Sym}^{n+1}((\mathbb Q^2)^*),\qquad
 H^2(N_P,E_n)=\det^{-2}\operatorname{Sym}^n((\mathbb Q^2)^*).
\]
The two opposite binary unipotents have no common invariant in positive
degree, so the second module has no $L_P$-invariants. The Levi has rational
cohomological dimension one, leaving only the mixed restriction. At a
binary cusp the mixed edge map is injective for the same dimension reason.
Flag vanishing therefore makes the plane class cuspidal.

Let $\xi_P$ and $\xi_Q$ be the collections of plane and line restrictions.
Let $T$ be the map taking plane cusp data to the line constant term of the
convergent cusp form sum constructed in Appendix~\ref{app:arithmetic-direct}.
Proposition~\ref{ar:prop:graph} gives $\xi_Q=T\xi_P$. It remains to show
that $\xi_P=0$.

In even degree the bad-plane
binary module has odd degree $n+1$, so its central $-I_2$ kills its
cohomology. Since all good-plane restrictions vanish, $\xi_P=0$ and hence
$\xi_Q=0$.

In odd degree the bad-plane datum is a level one cusp form, as
explained in Appendix~\ref{ar:sec:finite}. On each classical Hecke
eigenform its image at the good-line cusp is the nonzero scalar
\eqref{ar:eq:globalentry}, in the seed normalizations of
\eqref{ar:eq:seed}. Thus the good-line map is injective on the bad-plane space, whereas
the good-line restriction of $a_F$ is zero.
Again both $\xi_P$ and $\xi_Q$ vanish.

Lemma~\ref{lem:bad-line-coordinate} now gives $J_f=0$ as a polynomial,
not merely modulo coboundaries.

title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The signed-permutation orbits have support sizes one, two, and three. Their
stabilizers give the seed symmetries. The norm equations at
\[
 (0,0,1),\quad(1,1,0),\quad(1,1,1),\quad(1,0,1),\quad(1,0,0)
\]
give the five displayed equations. To see that they exhaust the fibers,
write $R(r)$ for the left side of \eqref{eq:fiber-norm}, and put
$D_{12}=\operatorname{diag}(-1,-1,1)$ and
$D_3=\operatorname{diag}(1,1,-1)$. Direct reindexing gives
\[
 R(rA)=R(r)\mid A,\qquad
 R(rD)=\chi_1(D)R(r)\mid D\quad(D=D_{12},D_3).
\]
The five representative orbits under $\langle A,D_{12},D_3\rangle$ have
sizes $2,2,4,12,6$, respectively. They partition the $26$ covectors.

label: lem:first-lift-norm
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:first-lift-norm}
Let $f\in\mathbb Q[x,y,z]$ be symmetric with $Nf=0$. If
$Q\in\mathbb Q[a,b,c]$ is symmetric in $a,b$, odd in $c$, and satisfies
\eqref{eq:mixed1}, then $N_{12}Q=0$.
head: environment

label: eq:common-denominator
title: Proof
body_md:
Let $\Delta_s$ translate $c$ by $s$ and subtract the original value. Put
\[
 R_1=f(a+c,-c,b),\quad R_2=f(c-b,-c,a-b),\quad
 R_3=f(b-a+c,-c,-a).
\]
The norm and symmetry give
\begin{equation}\label{eq:common-denominator}
 \Delta_{-b}\Delta_{b-a}R_1+
 \Delta_a\Delta_{b-a}R_2+\Delta_a\Delta_{-b}R_3=0.
\end{equation}
Appendix~\ref{app:finite-difference} gives the twelve-norm expansion of
this identity. By \eqref{eq:mixed1}, it becomes
\[
 \Delta_a\Delta_{-b}\Delta_{b-a}(N_{12}Q)=0.
\]
Over $\mathbb Q(a,b)$, each difference equals its nonzero step times $\partial_c$
times an invertible finite power series in $\partial_c$. Hence
$\partial_c^3N_{12}Q=0$, and oddness leaves $N_{12}Q=c\kappa(a,b)$.

Evaluate at $c=a$. With
$g_1=f(a,0,b)$, $g_2=f(-b,0,a-b)$, $g_3=f(b-a,0,-a)$, and
$h=f(a-b,-a,a-b)$, the mixed equation and symmetries give the three values
$g_1,g_2-h,-g_3$. Since
$(Nf)(a,b,0)=g_1+g_2+g_3$ and $(Nf)(b-a,0,-a)=2g_3+h$, we get
\[
 a\kappa=g_1+g_2-h-g_3
        =(g_1+g_2+g_3)-(2g_3+h)=0.
\]
Thus, we have $\kappa=0$.
head: environment

label: lem:residue-period
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:residue-period}
The map sending $q\in\mathcal B_{n+1}$ to the residue cycle represented by
\[
 F_q(a,b,c)=\frac{q(b,c)}a+\frac{q(a,c)}b+\frac{q(a,b)}c
\] identifies $\mathcal B_{n+1}$ with $H_3(G,\mathcal R_n\otimes\det)$.
Its inverse reads the literal residue at $a=0$, namely $q(b,c)$.
Let $\mathcal L_n$ be the image of $H_3(G,\mathcal M_n\otimes\det)$ in this
space. If $n>0$, then $[ac^n]q(a,c)=0$ for every $q\in\mathcal L_n$.
Moreover $\mathcal L_n$ is stable under the usual binary Hecke operators.
head: environment

label: eq:N-Fq
title: Proof
body_md:
A residue cycle is symmetric and separately odd, with finite hyperplane
support. Choose a noncoordinate supported primitive normal of maximal
height $|v_1|+|v_2|+|v_3|$, and normalize it by signed permutation to
$v=(\alpha,\beta,\gamma)$ with $\alpha,\beta>0$, $\gamma\ge0$.
The normals $vA=(\beta,-\alpha-\beta,\gamma)$ and
$vA^2=(-\alpha-\beta,\alpha,\gamma)$ remain primitive and have larger
height, so neither is supported. The norm relation at the hyperplane
normal to $v$ would then contain only its nonzero residue, a contradiction.
Thus only coordinate poles occur. Symmetry gives the representative $F_q$
in the statement, with $q$ symmetric and separately odd. Writing $d=a-b$,
direct substitution gives
\begin{equation}\label{eq:N-Fq}
 N_{12}F_q=K_q+\frac{N_2q(a,b)}c,\qquad
 K_q=\frac{a^2q(a,c)-b^2q(b,c)-d^2q(d,c)}{abd}.
\end{equation}
The numerator vanishes at $a=0$, $b=0$, and $a=b$. The three linear
factors $a,b,a-b$ are pairwise relatively prime, so their product divides
the numerator and $K_q$ is polynomial.
Consequently $F_q$ is norm-zero modulo polynomial coefficients if and
only if $N_2q=0$. Together with its symmetry and separate oddness, this
proves the converse as well as the residue identification.

It remains to determine the liftable residue subspace $\mathcal L_n$.
If this residue lifts to a top cycle, write the lift as $F_q+P$.
The polynomial remainder $P$ is symmetric and separately odd, with
$NP=-K_q$. To constrain $q$, put $\lambda=[ac^n]q(a,c)$ and compare the
$c^n$ coefficients. The numerator of $K_q$ contributes
\[
 \lambda\{a^3-b^3-(a-b)^3\}=3\lambda ab(a-b),
\]
so $[c^n]K_q=3\lambda$. Every monomial of $P$ is divisible by $ab$, and
$P$ has total degree $n$. Its $c$-degree is therefore at most $n-2$. The norm
acts only on $a,b$, so the same bound holds for $NP$. Comparing the
$c^n$ coefficient gives $3\lambda=0$ and therefore $\lambda=0$.

A Hecke correspondence consists of restriction, rational matrix transport,
and transfer. Sequence~\eqref{eq:residue-exact} commutes with all three:
rational matrices preserve numerator degree and pole order while permuting
hyperplanes, and the other maps are natural in the coefficients. Thus
liftable residues are Hecke-stable.
Let $T_3(p,1)$ be the double-coset operator of $\operatorname{diag}(1,1,p)$
and $T_2(p)$ the usual binary prime operator.
In the same literal residue coordinate, these operators satisfy
\begin{equation}\label{eq:Hecke-formula}
 T_3(p,1)=pT_2(p)+p^2I.
\end{equation}
Lemma~\ref{lem:literal-residue-comparison} identifies the literal residue
with the binary period coordinate. Appendix~\ref{app:Hecke-coordinate}
then computes the transfer using Hecke-equivariant Shapiro
\cite[Theorem 3.1]{AshDoud}. Naturality
makes $\mathcal L_n$ stable under the left side of \eqref{eq:Hecke-formula}.
Subtracting $p^2I$ and dividing by $p$ gives binary stability.
Only the nonzero coefficient of $T_2(p)$ is needed for stability.
A fixed scalar in the period comparison does not change this relation.

label: prop:alternating-even
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:alternating-even}
Every alternating even degree solution belongs to $U_n$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
\smallskip\noindent\emph{Vertex stabilizers.}
Assume $n>0$, since the constant case is zero. For the stabilizer calculation
use the group $K^\dagger$ and graph $\mathcal T^\dagger$ introduced in
Section~\ref{sec:symmetric}. The relative graph has two vertex
orbits, represented by the bad line $\mathbb Q e_1$ and bad plane
$\mathbb Q e_1+\mathbb Q e_2$, and two edge orbits: bad line in bad plane and bad line
in a good plane. Integral parabolic reduction modulo three proves this list
exhaustive. The vertex stabilizers are
\[
 H_P=\left\{\begin{pmatrix}A&u\\0&1\end{pmatrix}\right\},\qquad
 H_L=\left\{\begin{pmatrix}\eta&u\\0&D\end{pmatrix}\right\},
\]
where $A\in\mathrm{GL}_2(\mathbb Z)$, $u\in\mathbb Z^2$, $\eta=\pm1$, and
$D\in\Gamma_2=\{D\in\mathrm{GL}_2(\mathbb Z):(0,1)D=(0,1)\pmod3\}$.
The edge stabilizers are
\[
 H_{BB}=\left\{\begin{pmatrix}\eta_1&a&b\\0&\eta_2&c\\0&0&1\end{pmatrix}\right\},\qquad
 H_{BG}=\left\{\begin{pmatrix}\eta_1&a&b\\0&\eta_2&0\\0&3k&1\end{pmatrix}\right\},
\]
with integral entries and independent signs $\eta_i$.

Take $E=\operatorname{Sym}^n((\mathbb Q^3)^*)$ and write $\rho$ for its left
inverse substitution representation. The vertex radicals are
$N_P=\langle U_{13},U_{23}\rangle$ and
$N_L=\langle U_{12},U_{13}\rangle$. On dual polynomial coefficients, the generators act with
$\log\rho(U_{ij})=-x_j\partial_{x_i}$. For $N_P$,
the closed pairs are gradients of potentials, as in
Section~\ref{sec:ordinary}. Modulo exact pairs, restriction of the potential
to $z=0$ gives a binary form of degree $n+1$. Under a general diagonal
matrix this identification has an extra factor $d_3$, which is one on
$H_P$. For $N_L$, the contraction $(\alpha,\beta)\mapsto z\alpha-y\beta$ gives the binary form. Inverse conjugation on its two roots makes this
contraction transform by $\eta^{-1}\det D$ times the dual binary action.
In the table, $\operatorname{Sym}^r(x,y)^*$ abbreviates the degree $r$ binary
polynomials with inverse substitution action, and similarly for $y,z$.
These calculations give its first column.
\begin{table}[!htbp]
\centering
$\begin{array}{|c|c|c|}
\hline
&H^1(N,E)&H^2(N,E)\\\hline
 N_P&\operatorname{Sym}^{n+1}(x,y)^*&\det(A)^{-1}\operatorname{Sym}^n(x,y)^*\\
 N_L&\eta^{-1}\det(D)\operatorname{Sym}^{n+1}(y,z)^*&\eta^{-n-2}\det(D)\\
\hline
\end{array}$
\par\vspace{7pt}
\caption{Cohomology of the two vertex radicals with $E=\operatorname{Sym}^n((\mathbb Q^3)^*)$ and Levi actions.}
\label{tab:radical-cohomology}
\end{table}
\FloatBarrier
The $H^2$ column follows from the top cohomology formula for a rank two
lattice,
$H^2(N,E)=E_N\otimes\bigwedge^2(N\otimes\mathbb Q)^*$, using
$E_{N_P}=\mathbb Q[x,y]_n$ and $E_{N_L}=\mathbb Q x^n$.
These are coinvariants. The corresponding invariant spaces are
$E^{N_P}=\mathbb Q z^n$ and $E^{N_L}=\mathbb Q[y,z]_n$. These invariant spaces
enter the edge calculation below.
Both Levis are virtually free. Thus total degree two in Hochschild--Serre
has only $H^1(L,H^1(N,E))$ and $H^0(L,H^2(N,E))$.
At $H_P$, the central $-I_2$ acts by $-1$ on $H^1$ and positive binary
degree kills the $H^2$ invariants. At $H_L$, the independent line sign kills
$H^1$ and the reflection $\operatorname{diag}(-1,1)\in\Gamma_2$ kills $H^2$.
Hence, we have $H^2(H_P,E)=H^2(H_L,E)=0$.

\smallskip\noindent\emph{Edge stabilizers.}
For either edge radical, extend a rank two radical by its remaining cyclic
root. The exact sequence
$0\to H^1(\mathbb Z,E^N)\to H^1(N_{\rm edge},E)
\to H^1(N,E)^\mathbb Z\to0$ is equivariant for
$D_0=\{\operatorname{diag}(\eta_1,\eta_2,1)\}$.
A weight $(a_1,a_2,a_3)$ means the character
$\operatorname{diag}(d_1,d_2,d_3)\mapsto d_1^{a_1}d_2^{a_2}d_3^{a_3}$.
Table~\ref{tab:edge-weights} records the weights of the two
one-dimensional subquotients:
\begin{table}[!htbp]
\centering
$\begin{array}{|c|c|c|}
\hline
\text{edge type}&\text{first subquotient}&\text{second subquotient}\\
\hline
BB&(-1,1,-n)&(0,-n-1,1)\\
 BG&(0,1,-n-1)&(-1,-n,1)\\
\hline
\end{array}$
\par\vspace{7pt}
\caption{Weights of the two degree-one cohomology subquotients for each edge stabilizer. For even $n$, each row has a nontrivial sign character.}
\label{tab:edge-weights}
\end{table}
\FloatBarrier
For type $BB$, use $N_P$ and the remaining root $E_{12}$. The left term
of the five-term sequence comes from $E^{N_P}=\mathbb Q z^n$ and the dual of
$E_{12}$, giving $(-1,1,-n)$. The invariant potential in the right term is
$y^{n+1}$, with the extra $d_3$ factor, giving $(0,-n-1,1)$.
For type $BG$, use $N_L$ and $E_{32}$. The coinvariant of
$E^{N_L}=\mathbb Q[y,z]_n$ under $-y\partial_z$ is represented by $z^n$.
Including the root-dual factor gives $(0,1,-n-1)$. The right term is represented
by $y^{n+1}$ in $\eta^{-1}\det(D)\operatorname{Sym}^{n+1}(y,z)^*$, giving $(-1,-n,1)$.
For $H_{BG}$ the actual remaining lattice root is $3E_{32}$.
Multiplication of its logarithmic differential by the nonzero rational
scalar $3$ changes neither its kernel nor its cokernel.
Since $n$ is even, each weight has a nontrivial first or second sign.
Exact averaging gives $H^1(H_{BB},E)=H^1(H_{BG},E)=0$.

\smallskip\noindent\emph{Extension to the full graph.}
Put $\operatorname{St}^\dagger=H_1(\mathcal T^\dagger;\mathbb Q)$ and
$Q_0=\operatorname{St}/\operatorname{St}^\dagger$. The relative chain sequence and connectedness
of the two graphs give
\[
 0\longrightarrow Q_0\longrightarrow
 \mathbb Q[K^\dagger/H_{BB}]\oplus\mathbb Q[K^\dagger/H_{BG}]
 \longrightarrow
 \mathbb Q[K^\dagger/H_L]\oplus\mathbb Q[K^\dagger/H_P]\longrightarrow0.
\]
Applying $\operatorname{Hom}_{K^\dagger}(-,E)$ and Shapiro gives the exact segment
\[
\begin{split}
 H^1(H_{BB},E)\oplus H^1(H_{BG},E)
 &\longrightarrow\operatorname{Ext}_{K^\dagger}^1(Q_0,E)
 \longrightarrow H^2(H_L,E)\oplus H^2(H_P,E).
\end{split}
\]
The four vanishings make $\operatorname{Ext}_{K^\dagger}^1(Q_0,E)=0$. The sequence
$0\to\operatorname{St}^\dagger\to\operatorname{St}\to Q_0\to0$ shows that
$\operatorname{Hom}_{K^\dagger}(\operatorname{St},E)\to\operatorname{Hom}_{K^\dagger}(\operatorname{St}^\dagger,E)$ is surjective.
Returning to the original coordinates, we apply
Proposition~\ref{thm:boundary-evaluation} on the identity
apartment. This value is the original polynomial, so it belongs to $U_n$.

label: mf:thm:main
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{mf:thm:main}
Let $f\in\mathbb Z[x,y,z]$ be alternating, with every monomial of odd total degree.
If $Nf\in4\mathbb Z[x,y,z]$, then $f\in2\mathbb Z[x,y,z]$.
Consequently, an alternating homogeneous solution of $Nf=0$ in odd degree
over any characteristic zero field is zero.

title: Proof
body_md:
Expand the left side into $54$ terms. Identify triples of linear forms that differ only by a permutation,
which does not change their value on a symmetric polynomial.
There are exactly $27$ resulting triples,
each occurring twice. They cancel in characteristic two. The lists in
\eqref{mf:eq:Tlist} and the three substitutions defining $\overline N$ completely
specify these pairings.

title: Proof
body_md:
Two lifts with the same symmetry differ by $2h$ with that symmetry.
The reduction $\overline h$ is symmetric in either case, so the change in
\eqref{mf:eq:beta} is $\Pi\overline N\overline h=0$ by
Lemma~\ref{mf:lem:cancellation}.

If an integral polynomial $D$ is invariant modulo two, its square is
invariant modulo four: $(D+2E)^2\equiv D^2\pmod4$.
Consequently, the integral squares of the three polynomials in
\eqref{mf:eq:invariants} are invariant modulo four under the substitutions
in $N$. Their reductions are also invariant under every substitution in
\eqref{mf:eq:Tlist}. Multiplying a lift by any polynomial in those squares
therefore commutes with division of its norm by two followed by reduction
and application of $\Pi$. These squares generate $R_2$.

$1,q,p,pq$ of $R_0$. Lemma~\ref{mf:lem:well-defined} therefore reduces

\[
 V_{4j}=L_j,\quad V_{4j+1}=qL_j,\quad
 V_{4j+2}=pL_j,\quad V_{4j+3}=pqL_j.

above to form each norm, divide its even coefficients by two, and apply
the $18$ substitutions in \eqref{mf:eq:Tlist}. Exact expansion gives
$\beta_-(V_\nu)=V_\nu+\beta_+(V_\nu)$ in every column.

\begin{array}{c|l@{\qquad}c|l}
\nu&\beta_+(V_\nu)&\nu&\beta_+(V_\nu)\\ \hline
16&V_{12}&17&V_8+V_{13}\\

The image of $U$ has no $L_5$ or $L_7$ coefficient. Applying $U$ again
therefore leaves only $L_0,L_2,L_3$ terms, and $U$ kills those terms.

title: Proof
body_md:
Reduce $f$ modulo two, obtaining $v$. Alternation becomes symmetry and
$Nf\equiv0\pmod4$ gives $\overline N v=0$. Using $f$ itself as the lift in
\eqref{mf:eq:beta}, we get $\beta_-(v)=0$.
By Lemma~\ref{mf:lem:beta}, this gives $(I+U)v=0$.

A nonzero rational alternating solution of odd degree can be scaled to
a primitive integer polynomial. The integral assertion would make all
its coefficients even, a contradiction. In each fixed degree the norm
and symmetry conditions are a finite rational linear system. Its kernel
remains zero after extension to any characteristic zero field.

title: Proposition
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
In monomial bases, the defining identities are finite linear systems over
$\mathbb Q$. Every $\mathbb Q$-algebra is flat over $\mathbb Q$, so extension of scalars
preserves their kernels. This proves the two isomorphisms and applies
unchanged after imposing symmetry or parity. Restriction to a coordinate
plane and cyclic summation have rational matrices, so they commute with
extension of scalars as well.

title: Proof
body_md:
Lemma~\ref{lem:sector-decomp} reduces to four homogeneous symmetry-parity
sectors. Section~\ref{sec:symmetric} proves the symmetric classification,
Proposition~\ref{prop:alternating-even} gives alternating even degree
support, and Theorem~\ref{mf:thm:main} gives alternating odd degree
vanishing. Thus every solution has two-variable support and every odd
piece vanishes. The symmetric summand is $f(X,Y,0)$, and its converse
follows from the pairwise cancellation at the end of Section~\ref{sec:symmetric}.

The operator $\partial_x\partial_y\partial_z$ kills exactly the monomials
missing a variable. The remaining monomials have distinct nonzero
derivatives in characteristic zero, proving the differential formulation.

Proposition~\ref{prop:coefficient-base-change} writes every solution over
a characteristic zero field as a linear combination of rational solutions.
It therefore preserves support and odd degree vanishing. Its compatibility
with restriction preserves the symmetric classification and the unique
choice $q=f(X,Y,0)$. This proves both theorems.

label: lem:alternating-classification
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:alternating-classification}
Let $F$ be a field of characteristic zero and let $n>0$ be even. An
alternating polynomial $f\in F[x,y,z]_n$ is a solution if and only if
$f=\Phi(q)$, where $q\in F[X,Y]_n$ is alternating, even in each variable,
zero on both axes, and satisfies \eqref{eq:binary-period-intro}.
In that case, we have $q(X,Y)=f(X,Y,0)$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Suppose that $f$ is a solution. Theorem~\ref{thm:main} gives its two-variable
support. The norm at $(0,0,z)$ gives $3f(0,0,z)=0$, so cyclicity removes all
pure powers. Every remaining monomial is supported on exactly two variables.
Cyclicity therefore gives
$f=\Phi(q),\quad q(X,Y)=f(X,Y,0)$.
The polynomial $q$ is alternating and vanishes on the axes. Restriction of
the norm to $z=0$ gives $N_2q=0$.

It remains to prove separate evenness. Put
$r(u,v)=q(u,v)-q(-u,v)$. Expanding $N\Phi(q)$ and using alternation and
$N_2q=0$ gives
\begin{equation}\label{eq:alternating-additivity}
 r(y,z)-r(x,z)+r(x-y,z)=0.
\end{equation}
Indeed, after removing the three terms of $N_2q(x,y)$, the six remaining
terms are
\[
 q(y,z)-q(x,z)+q(x-y,z)-q(-y,z)+q(-x,z)-q(y-x,z),
\]
which is the left side of \eqref{eq:alternating-additivity}.
Thus, we have $r(u+v,z)=r(u,z)+r(v,z)$. Differentiating in $v$ at $v=0$ shows that
$\partial_ur(u,z)$ is independent of $u$. Since $r(0,z)=0$, we have
$r(u,z)=u h(z)$ for a polynomial $h$.

Since $q$ is alternating and homogeneous of even total degree,
we have $r(v,u)=-r(u,v)$.
On the diagonal, this means that $2u h(u)=0$, so $h=0$ in characteristic zero.
Hence, we have $q(-u,v)=q(u,v)$. Alternation gives evenness in the other variable.
Conversely, for a binary polynomial with these properties, the three
terms of $N_2q$ sum to zero and the six terms displayed above cancel. Hence
$\Phi(q)$ is a solution. The axis normalization recovers $q$ on $z=0$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The degree zero spaces are zero. The relation $q(X,Y)+q(-Y,X)=0$, applied
twice, gives $q(-X,-Y)=q(X,Y)$. Thus $\mathscr P_n^0=0$ when $n$ is odd,
as is $W_n$ by Theorem~\ref{thm:main}.

Let $n>0$ be even. The involution $q(X,Y)\mapsto q(-X,Y)$ preserves
the binary period relations \cite[Section~2, (2.2)--(2.4)]{PasolPopa}.
To match conventions, homogenize by $P(X)\mapsto Y^nP(X/Y)$.
The matrix $U^2$ in that reference gives our substitution
$(X,Y)\mapsto(-Y,X-Y)$. Since $U^3=-I$ and $-I$ acts trivially in
even degree, the two three-term norms agree. The involution also preserves
the axis conditions, so $(q(X,Y)\pm q(-X,Y))/2$ gives the two normalized
parity projections.

This is a statement about binary periods, not coordinate sign projections
of the ternary norm. The two-term relation makes the odd part symmetric
and separately odd, and the even part alternating and separately even.
In the notation of Section~\ref{sec:polynomial}, we have
$\mathscr P_n^{0,\mathrm{odd}}=\mathcal B_n$ and $\mathscr P_n^{0,\mathrm{ev}}=\mathcal B_n^0$.
Theorem~\ref{thm:symmetric-classification} and
Lemma~\ref{lem:alternating-classification} identify these spaces with the
two sectors exhausting $W_n$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:sector-decomp}. Both inverse
maps are $\Phi$. Since the summands vanish on the axes, its restriction to
$z=0$ is exactly $q$. This proves the rational isomorphism and uniqueness.
Compatibility with restriction and $\Phi$ in
Proposition~\ref{prop:coefficient-base-change} extends the result to $F$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Eichler--Shimura identifies cusp forms with the two period spaces modulo
coboundaries \cite[Theorem~2.1]{PasolPopa}. At level one the coboundary
space is spanned by $X^n-Y^n$. It lies in the even part, and
\eqref{eq:even-period-normalization} selects its unique axis-normalized
representative. Thus the two period maps give
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 S_{n+2}&\xrightarrow{\sim}\mathscr P_n^{0,\mathrm{odd}}\otimes\mathbb C,
 &h&\mapsto r_h^{\mathrm{odd}},\\
 S_{n+2}&\xrightarrow{\sim}\mathscr P_n^{0,\mathrm{ev}}\otimes\mathbb C,
 &h&\mapsto r_h^{\mathrm{ev},0}.
 \end{aligned}
\]
Composing with $\Phi$ proves the claimed
identifications. The coefficient-extension proposition transfers the
complex dimensions to every characteristic zero field. Odd degrees and
degree zero vanish by the classification. Finally,
the graded space $S_*:=\bigoplus_{k\ge0}S_k$ satisfies
$S_* =\Delta_{\mathrm{mod}}\mathbb C[E_4,E_6]$, where $E_4,E_6$ are the
normalized Eisenstein series of weights four and six and
$\Delta_{\mathrm{mod}}$ is the weight twelve discriminant cusp form. This gives
$\sum_k\dim S_k\,t^k=t^{12}/((1-t^4)(1-t^6))$
\cite[Chapter VII]{SerreArithmetic}. Shift $k$ to $n+2$ and multiply by two
to obtain \eqref{eq:W-Hilbert}.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
By the
classification, each nonzero sector is $\Phi(q)$ for a normalized binary
period of one of the two parities, and in both cases we have
\[
 q(u,u)=q(u,-u)=0,\qquad q(-u,v)=-q(v,u).
\]
For the symmetric case the first diagonal vanishing follows by evaluating
the binary norm at $(u,u)$ and using the axis values. For the alternating
case it follows directly from alternation. The other identities follow
from the parity conditions. Thus, we have
$\Phi(q)(u,-u,v)=0$.
Cyclicity supplies the factors $x+y$, $y+z$, and $z+x$.
The construction of $L(q)$ in \eqref{eq:polynomial-lift} already proves divisibility
by $x+y+z$ for either symmetry. The four linear factors are pairwise
nonassociate, so their product $D$ divides each sector and every solution.

To prove that $D$ is the entire common divisor, use the degree ten basis
$f_{\mathrm{s}}=\Phi(q_{\mathrm{s}})$ and
$f_{\mathrm{a}}=\Phi(q_{\mathrm{a}})$ from the introduction. Expansion gives
\begin{equation}\label{eq:sharp-divisor-factorization}
\begin{split}
 f_{\mathrm{a}}={}&D(x,y,z)(x-y)(x-z)(y-z)
 \cdot(x-y-z)(x-y+z)(x+y-z).
\end{split}
\end{equation}
All ten linear factors are distinct. On the other hand, we have
\[
 f_{\mathrm{s}}(u,u,v)=2q_{\mathrm{s}}(u,v),\qquad
 f_{\mathrm{s}}(u+v,u,v)=2q_{\mathrm{s}}(u,v).
\]
Neither is identically zero, and symmetry of $f_{\mathrm{s}}$ shows
that none of the six additional factors in
\eqref{eq:sharp-divisor-factorization} divides it. Therefore, we have
$\gcd(f_{\mathrm{s}},f_{\mathrm{a}})=D$ up to a nonzero constant.
Since both are solutions and $D$ divides every solution, the result follows.

label: lem:bad-link-generators
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:bad-link-generators}
The link $L_b$ is connected and $H_1(L_b;\mathbb Q)=0$.
Its second homology is generated by the tetrahedral boundaries
\[
 \partial[u_k,u_{k+1},v_l,v_{l+1}]
\]
over base edges, and by the prism boundaries joining $\theta_{k,l}$
to $\theta_{k+1,l}$ or to $\theta_{k,l+1}$ over augmented base triangles.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Attach a $3$-cell along each displayed sphere, obtaining $L_b^+$.
Filter this complex by the dimension of its image in $Z$:
\[
 F_{-1}=\varnothing\subset F_0\subset F_1\subset F_2=L_b^+.
\]
We compute the homology of each successive pair.

Over a vertex, the path $P_u$ is contractible. Over an edge $[u,v]$,
the tetrahedral cells complete the join $P_u*P_v$. Relative to the
endpoint fibers, the contribution is
\[
 H_i(P_u*P_v,P_u\sqcup P_v;\mathbb Q)
   =\begin{cases}\mathbb Q,&i=1,\\0,&i\ne1.\end{cases}
\]
This follows from the long exact sequence of the pair: the join is
contractible and the two endpoint fibers are contractible components.
Any cross-edge from $P_u$ to $P_v$ represents the generator.

Over an augmented base triangle, the relative complex has only the
coherent triangles and the prism cells. It is
\begin{equation}\label{eq:link-relative-grid}
 \mathbb Q[\mathcal E(\mathbb Z^2)]\xrightarrow{\delta}\mathbb Q[\mathbb Z^2],
 \qquad\delta[\nu,\nu']=\theta_{\nu'}-\theta_\nu,
\end{equation}
in degrees three and two, where $\mathcal E(\mathbb Z^2)$ consists of the
oriented horizontal and vertical edges of the integer grid.
The side faces disappear in the relative quotient. Connectedness of
the grid makes $\operatorname{coker}\delta=\mathbb Q$, while its kernel
contributes only in degree three.

Consequently, through total degree two the spectral sequence
$E^1_{p,q}=H_{p+q}(F_p,F_{p-1};\mathbb Q)$ is concentrated in the row
$q=0$. This row is the simplicial chain complex of $Z$: cross-edges
have the expected endpoints, and coherent triangles have the expected
three boundary edges. The only additional term, $E^1_{2,1}$, has
zero possible targets $E^1_{1,1}$ and $E^2_{0,2}$. Since $Z$ is
contractible, $L_b^+$ is connected and has zero homology in degrees
one and two.

Only $3$-cells were added to $L_b$. The long exact sequence of
$(L_b^+,L_b)$ therefore preserves connectedness and first homology,
and gives a surjection
\[
 H_3(L_b^+,L_b;\mathbb Q)\longrightarrow H_2(L_b;\mathbb Q).
\]
The generators on the left map to the attaching spheres, which are
precisely the two families in the statement.

label: lem:literal-residue-comparison
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The stabilizer of $a=0$ in $\mathrm{GL}_3(\mathbb Q)$ consists of
$g=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}\lambda&0\\u&C\end{smallmatrix}\right)$.
On the determinant-twisted residue its action is
$q\mapsto\det(C)q(C(b,c))$. Its integral radical $U=\mathbb Z^2$ acts trivially
on that fiber. Right homology acts on $H_2(U,\mathbb Q)$ by inverse conjugation,
with factor $\lambda^2/\det C$. The combined factor is therefore $\lambda^2$.
On the integral Levi this is one. The only total-degree-three
Hochschild--Serre term is $(1,2)$, giving
\[
 H_3(P_H,\mathcal R_{n,H}\otimes\det)
   \cong H_1(\mathrm{GL}_2(\mathbb Z),D_{n+1}).
\]
This is $\kappa$. Shapiro is Hecke-equivariant for this
finite-support system \cite[Theorem 3.1]{AshDoud}. The following cell
calculation specifies the coordinate. The standard
binary well-rounded edge has minimum-one Gram matrices
$C(t)=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}1&t\\t&1\end{smallmatrix}\right)$, $|t|\le1/2$.
A coordinate sign flip reverses the edge, whereas a coordinate swap fixes
it. The coefficient is separately odd and symmetric. The three
edges meeting at a hexagonal vertex give the binary norm.
For a minimum-one binary well-rounded form $C$ and $w\in\mathbb R^2$, put
\[
 \delta_C(w)^2=\min_{z\in\mathbb Z^2}(w-z)^tC(w-z),\qquad
 G(w,C)=\begin{pmatrix}1+w^tCw-\delta_C(w)^2&w^tC\\Cw&C\end{pmatrix}.
\]
For $C(t)$ the covering radius squared is $1/(2(1+|t|))\le1/2$.
For $t\ge0$ this follows from the Voronoi inequalities
$|w_1+tw_2|,|tw_1+w_2|\le1/2$ and $|w_1-w_2|\le1$.
All vertices have that squared length. A sign flip handles $t\le0$.
Thus the Schur complement is positive.

Translate $w$ into the Voronoi cell of zero. The squared length of an
integral vector $(k,z)$ for $G(w,C)$ is
$k^2(1-w^tCw)+(z+kw)^tC(z+kw)$.
For $k=0$ the binary minimum gives the lower bound one. For $k=\pm1$,
the same bound follows from the Voronoi inequality. If $|k|\ge2$, the first
term alone is at least $k^2/2\ge2$.
The vector $(1,0)$ and two independent binary shortest vectors have length
one, so this is a ternary well-rounded form.
For $p=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}\eta&0\\u&D\end{smallmatrix}\right)$, with $\eta=\pm1$,
put $C'=D^tCD$, $w'=D^{-1}(u+\eta w)$. Then a direct computation gives
$p^tG(w,C)p=G(w',C')$.
The map is injective, and its image is the union of integral parabolic
translates of the standard ternary top cell: reduce the binary block and
translate $w$ to its Voronoi polygon. Conversely, the inequalities for
$(1,z)$ in that cell are exactly the same Voronoi inequalities.

Let $W_3$ be the ternary retract and $W_2$ the binary retract. The map
$i:(w,C)\mapsto G(w,C)$ identifies this with $\mathbb R^2\times W_2$ and is
$P_H$-equivariant. Both this core and $W_3$ are contractible. After equivariant
subdivision, their augmented cellular chains are rational projective
resolutions for $P_H$: the cell stabilizers are finite and averaging is
exact. The cellular inclusion lifts the identity of the trivial module,
so the comparison theorem for resolutions identifies its induced map with
the canonical group homology map \cite[Chapter~I, Sections~7--8]{Brown}.

The radical acts trivially on the residue fiber. Quotienting its
$\mathbb R^2$ coordinate by $\mathbb Z^2$ gives the oriented torus that represents
$H_2(U,\mathbb Q)$. Fiber integration on the cellular cross product is
$[\mathbb Z^2\backslash\mathbb R^2]\otimes(e\otimes q) \longmapsto e\otimes q$, where $e$ is an oriented binary edge and the torus has lattice volume one.
Since the Levi has rational cohomological dimension one, bidegree $(1,2)$
is the only term in total degree three. This fiber map is therefore
precisely the Hochschild--Serre map $\kappa$.

For the standard binary edge, take $w$ in the Voronoi cell of zero.
Then $\delta_C(w)^2=w^tCw$ and the first diagonal entry of $G(w,C)$ is one.
The image is the standard ternary cell, and its residue coefficient at
$a=0$ is the same polynomial $q(b,c)$ throughout the fiber. No derivative
or change of the variables $b,c$ occurs in integration. The Jacobian from
$(w_1,w_2,t)$ to $(Cw,t)$ is positive. The ternary cell stabilizer has order
$48$ and the stabilizer also preserving $H$ has order $16$. Their three
cosets give the three coordinate residues in $F_q$. Cellular averaging and
orientation can consequently change this calculation only by one common
nonzero scalar. This proves the commutative diagram after the stated
normalization.

Finally, the binary modular symbol from $0$ to $i\infty$ crosses the
standard edge once. Pairing with an arbitrary dual binary coefficient
identifies its edge coefficient with the odd part of
$\int_0^{i\infty}h(z)(zc-b)^{n+1}\,dz$, with the same orientation
normalization. Thus the comparison is the usual period map in the literal
variables \cite[Theorem 2.1 and Section 5]{PasolPopa}.

label: ar:prop:coercivity
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{ar:prop:coercivity}
For every $n>0$ there is a constant $c_n>0$, independent of $\Gamma$,
such that every compactly supported smooth $E$-valued form on $X_\Gamma$
satisfies
\begin{equation}\label{ar:eq:coercivity}
 \|D\omega\|^2+\|D^*\omega\|^2\ge c_n\|\omega\|^2.
\end{equation}
Consequently the natural map
$H_c^2(X_\Gamma,E)\longrightarrow H^2(X_\Gamma,E)$ is zero.
The conclusion holds for either determinant twist after descent from a
neat normal subgroup.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The Cartan involution $g\mapsto(g^{-1})^{\mathsf t}$ exchanges
$\operatorname{Sym}^n\mathbb C^3$ with its dual. For $t>1$, the matrix
$\operatorname{diag}(t,t,t^{-2})$ has largest eigenvalues $t^n$ and
$t^{2n}$ on these two spaces, respectively. They are therefore
nonisomorphic when $n>0$.

The proof of \cite[Lemma~4.1]{BergeronVenkatesh} gives a positive constant
$\varepsilon_E$ such that
\[
 \Lambda_{E^*}-\Lambda_\pi\ge\varepsilon_E
 \quad\text{whenever}\quad
 \operatorname{Hom}_{K_c}(\textstyle\bigwedge^j\mathfrak p_{\mathbb C}\otimes E^*,\pi)\ne0,
\]
for any irreducible unitary representation $\pi$ of $G_{\mathbb R}$ and any $j$.
Here $\Lambda$ is the eigenvalue of the Casimir, the invariant
second order operator. We use the estimate for unitary representations,
not the reference's compact quotient conclusion. Kuga's formula
\cite[(3.6.1)]{BergeronVenkatesh} identifies the Laplacian on the indicated
cochains with $\Lambda_{E^*}-\Lambda_\pi$, since $E$ and $E^*$ have the same
Casimir scalar. The reference uses the Killing metric, which is a positive
multiple of ours, so rescaling changes only the positive constant.

Now identify square-integrable forms with
\[
 L^2\Omega^j(X_\Gamma,E)
 \cong\operatorname{Hom}_{K_c}(\textstyle\bigwedge^j\mathfrak p_{\mathbb C}\otimes E^*,
                         L^2(\Gamma\backslash G_{\mathbb R})).
\]
The right regular representation is a direct integral of irreducible
unitary representations, the continuous analogue of a direct sum. The
uniform bound controls every constituent, including the continuous
spectrum, and gives \eqref{ar:eq:coercivity}. Taking the smaller constant
for $E$ and its dual gives $c_n$ for both.

On the complete quotient $X_\Gamma$, choose compactly supported cutoffs
$\chi_R\to1$ with $|d\chi_R|\le C/R$. The commutators with $D,D^*$ are
exterior multiplication and contraction by $d\chi_R$. These bounds and
local smoothing show that closing the differential on
compactly supported forms gives its distributional domain, and likewise
for the adjoint. The estimate extends to the closed quadratic form.
Its self-adjoint Laplacian $\Delta_j$ therefore has a bounded inverse $G_j$.

The identity $D^2=0$ makes $D$ intertwine the adjacent Laplacians and their
resolvents on this closed complex. For compactly supported closed
$\omega$ of degree two, we have $DG_2\omega=G_3D\omega=0$, and hence
\[
 \omega=(DD^*+D^*D)G_2\omega=D(D^*G_2\omega).
\]
Local elliptic regularity makes this primitive smooth. It need not have
compact support, which is exactly the claimed vanishing of the map to
ordinary cohomology. Determinant twists are trivial on $\operatorname{SL}_3$, and
finite group averaging descends a primitive from a neat normal cover.

label: ar:lem:stokes
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Use smooth representatives on $\overline X_\Gamma$, whose inclusion of
the interior is a homotopy equivalence. The cup product has degree four,
and the integral of its restriction over the oriented boundary is zero
by Stokes's theorem.

We identify the integral before discarding any corner coordinate.
Let $F_P,F_Q$ be the two unions of maximal faces and let $F_B$ be the
union of their flag intersections. Use collar thickenings when forming a
cover. A de Rham model for the boundary is the mapping cone
\[
 \Omega^r(F_P;E)\oplus\Omega^r(F_Q;E)\oplus\Omega^{r-1}(F_B;E),\qquad
 d(\alpha,\beta,u)=(d\alpha,d\beta,
             \alpha|_{F_B}-\beta|_{F_B}-du).
\]
Choose closed face representatives. Their restrictions to a flag collar
are exact, since the collar retracts onto the flag and the restricted
cohomology classes are zero. Extend a primitive with a cutoff, and
subtract its differential. The new face representatives vanish on a
smaller collar. After the same change of representative in the mapping
cone, its corner coordinate $u$ is closed.

The corresponding corner class is represented on the boundary by
$d\chi\wedge u$, with $u$ pulled back from the flag. Choose the same
transverse cutoff $\chi$ for the two classes. Face--corner products vanish
because the face representatives vanish on its support. Corner--corner
products vanish because $d\chi\wedge d\chi=0$. Distinct flag collars can
be taken disjoint, since there is no triple intersection of maximal faces
in rank three. The remaining integral is the sum of the two compactly
supported face pairings. Stokes therefore gives \eqref{ar:eq:stokes}.
This argument changes representatives rather than assuming that the
original corner cochain is zero. Finite averaging descends the identity.

label: ar:lem:seed
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{ar:lem:seed}
The form $\omega_h$ is closed and is equivariant for $\Gamma_P$ with
coefficients $E$. Its radical class is the binary degree $n+1$ cusp form
class, up to a nonzero scalar.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Put $\beta=du_1-\tau du_2$. Then, we have
\[
 d\mathcal B=(Y-u_2Z)d\tau+Z\beta,\qquad
 d\beta=-d\tau\wedge du_2.
\]
Each term in $d(h\mathcal B^n\beta\wedge d\tau)$ has a repeated factor
$\beta$ or $d\tau$, and is zero. A radical translation replaces $u$ by
$u+v$, and its coefficient action replaces $(X,Y)$ by
$(X-v_1Z,Y-v_2Z)$, proving equivariance under the lattice.

For the Levi calculation let
$g=\operatorname{diag}(A,t)$,
$A=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}a&b\\c&d\end{smallmatrix}\right)$, and
$\delta=\det A>0$. We have $u'=Au/t$ and
$\tau'=(a\tau+b)/(c\tau+d)$. Direct substitution gives
\[
 \mathcal B(u',\tau',\mathbf X)
    =\frac{\delta}{c\tau+d}\mathcal B(u,\tau,g^{-1}\mathbf X),\quad
 \beta'=\frac{\delta}{t(c\tau+d)}\beta,\quad
 d\tau'=\frac{\delta}{(c\tau+d)^2}d\tau.
\]
After including the determinant factor in $\rho$, this becomes
\begin{equation}\label{ar:eq:seed-transform}
 g^*\omega_h=\rho(g)\omega_{\delta^{k/2}(h|_k A)}.
\end{equation}
At the neat integral stabilizer, $t=\delta=1$, and the modular transformation
law proves equivariance. The finite reflection projection supplies the
corresponding full-level statement.

At $u=0$, the radical cochain is
$(\tau Y-X)^n(1,-\tau)$. In the potential description of plane-radical
cohomology, it is the gradient of
$-(\tau Y-X)^{n+1}/(n+1)$. This is precisely the required binary
coefficient, with its nonzero scalar specified. Eichler--Shimura theory
\cite[Theorem~2.1]{PasolPopa} therefore shows that the holomorphic and
antiholomorphic seeds span
$\mathcal C_P(E)$ after including all plane cusps and finite reflections.

label: ar:prop:convergence
title: Proposition
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
At the base point write $\gamma=pk_0$ with $p$ in plane coordinates and
$k_0\in\mathrm{SO}(3)$. The bottom row of $p$ is $(0,0,t)$, so
$t=\|e_3^*\gamma\|$ and $\det A=t^{-1}$. In the coefficient transported
pullback, the factor $\rho(p)$ in \eqref{ar:eq:seed-transform} cancels.
The remaining compact action has bounded norm. Furthermore,
\[
 |(h|_k A)(i)|
   =\left(\frac{\delta}{|ci+d|^2}\right)^{k/2}|h(Ai)|
   =(\Im Ai)^{k/2}|h(Ai)|
\]
is bounded. Equation~\eqref{ar:eq:seed-transform} therefore bounds the
norm of a summand by $Ct^{-k/2}$.
The cosets inject, with a bounded multiplicity depending only on the
congruence subgroup, into primitive integral bottom rows. Consequently, we have
\[
 \sum_{\gamma}\|\text{summand at }\gamma\|
 \le C'\sum_{0\ne v\in\mathbb Z^3}\|v\|^{-k/2}<\infty,
\]
since $k/2>3$. On a compact set, the norms of $vg$ and $v$ are uniformly
comparable. Rational conjugation changes the lattice by fixed denominators
and does not change convergence.

For derivatives, write $k_0g=p(k_0,g)k_1(k_0,g)$ for
$k_0\in\mathrm{SO}(3)$ and $g$ in a fixed neighborhood of the identity.
The parabolic and compact factors, and each fixed derivative of them,
are bounded uniformly in $k_0$. The parabolic character
$\delta^{k/2}$ is unchanged. A right derivative therefore produces
finitely many binary invariant derivatives of the cusp vector,
compact coefficient matrices, and constants from the character.
The binary derivatives are compositions of weight raising,
weight lowering, and rotation operators. Each is bounded in its
normalized weight: this follows from smoothness on the compact part of
a fundamental region and from the exponentially convergent Fourier
expansion at every cusp. Thus the same summable row majorant applies
to every fixed smooth seminorm. Termwise differentiation is legitimate,
and Lemma~\ref{ar:lem:seed} proves closedness.

label: ar:prop:graph
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{ar:prop:graph}
Let $n\ge4$. If a global degree two class with coefficients $E$ has only
mixed cuspidal maximal face restrictions $(\xi_P,\xi_Q)$ and zero flag
restrictions, then $\xi_Q=T\xi_P$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Pair the class with $\mathcal E_Q^\vee(\eta)$ in
Lemma~\ref{ar:lem:stokes}, for arbitrary $\eta\in\mathcal C_Q(E^*)$:
\[
 \langle\xi_P,T^\vee\eta\rangle_P+\langle\xi_Q,\eta\rangle_Q=0.
\]
Pair $\mathcal E_P(\xi_P)$ with the same dual class:
\[
 \langle\xi_P,T^\vee\eta\rangle_P+\langle T\xi_P,\eta\rangle_Q=0.
\]
Subtract and use the perfect line pairing \eqref{ar:eq:facepair}.
This proves graph containment without computing the dimension of the
global image.
